utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. It's Carmela Javier, Lorna Bolton, and Mark Harmon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom -- in and about the courtroom. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, and our intern Kay Marshall. I'm Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Ms. Prosecution, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness for the Prosecution, Your Honour, will be Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess he is coming by videolink.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Haider, good afternoon. Mr. Sacirbey, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sacirbey, before we start and before I hand you over to the counsel for the Prosecution, the Chamber has been approached by Registry indicating that you request to have your lawyers with you while you testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Just to let you know your request has been granted, you can have your lawyers next to you before you start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the witness's request, in the United States, as a matter of practice, a witness is allowed confer with counsel not only during their testimony but also when they are not testifying, and with regard to that particular practice, I trust that the court will make an order that although Mr. Sacirbey can have his counsel present, his counsel may not communicate with him whatsoever in any respect from this time forward unless we reach an issue with regard to matters concerning his potential criminal liabilities, which is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, my understanding was that that's the basis for wanting his lawyers to be present with him, and if he wasn't able to communicate with his lawyer, it would nullify the very presence of the lawyer. So I would expect that the lawyer would only come in when matters of self-incrimination arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will make that warning before we start --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to the lawyers and to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless, then perhaps we could have some further understanding because unless the Prosecution intends to raise this matter with Mr. Sacirbey during the case in chief, it would be inappropriate for the lawyer to be present during that time unless they are going to be touching about those matter that revolve around any issues concerning his self-incrimination and his privilege against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understood him, the Prosecution's motion that it actually wanted to exclude that very kind of examination, I wouldn't expect them to go and do something that they asked not to have done. Madam Bolton, if you can place on record your shaking of the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have no intention of going into that area in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is. And with that in mind I would ask that his lawyer be excluded from the proceedings until my cross-examination because that would be the time that issue would come up. If it comes up it comes up at the point in time that he would be concerned about being involved in the answers that would incriminate him. Other than that, his presence is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no difficulty with him not communicating about any matters that come up in chief. I suppose that like any other interested member of the public, the counsel would be entitled to be present in the sense of listening to the proceedings, but I certainly don't expect them to be communicating. And, of course, as counsel I would expect them to abide by any warning you gave about communications and the limits of communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Guy-Smith, just for the free flow of the proceedings without having to stop to allow lawyer to come in. Obviously, they could have been very much in the gallery and listening, and so if they are sitting next to him provided they don't discuss with him, that they don't communicate with him, do you have any objection to them being there next to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I can see him and I take it that the attorney -- if at some point he could identify himself, I take it that he will be able to remain stone-faced throughout these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My name is Peter Guirguis. I'm from the International Law Firm of Fulbright & Jaworski, and I'm here to represent Mr. Sacirbey. I am familiar with the court's rules and I understand that I'm not to communicate with him about the substance of his testimony, I appreciate the opportunity to be hear with him and hear the direct testimony so that I can have context for any issues as they are raised on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said your name is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Peter Guirguis, last name is spelled G-u-i-r-g-u-i-s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are -- okay. Mr. Guirguis, thank you so much. I did want to say to you that -- yes, you did mention it, that you are not supposed to talk to the witness while he is testifying. The only time you may intervene is if and when any questions that may cause him to self-incriminate arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. I'll only discuss those matters with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Only if I might add, I'm referring to the Chamber's decision paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are on paragraph 5, paragraph 13 or line 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm referring to the Chamber's decision with regard to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to say, yes, that order was given in line with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal without having had the benefit of the request from the witness himself for the presence of his lawyer in court, and the only reason that we change that part now was simply because of that request. Do I understand you to be saying that notwithstanding the ruling, sir, that you still insist that you are re-opening the matter? You want a reconsideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not re-opening the matter. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that based -- based upon the Trial Chamber's previous ruling, in the ostensible purpose for counsel to be there, it is inappropriate for counsel to be there at this time. I am not suggesting that during cross-examination it would be inappropriate for counsel to be there, I believe that it would be. And as a matter of fact I would encourage it. I come from that tradition. But at this point in time it would not be, but I remain in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, do you have any final things to say on this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Simply that again I reiterate that there's -- a Registrar is present, so if there were to be any difficulties or any suggestion that Mr. Guirguis were communicating inappropriately, he would actually be there to see it. And if Mr. Guirguis, if he were any other member of the public, would be entitled to watch the proceedings, and he has indicated that he like to be present so that if any issues arise in cross-examination, notwithstanding the fact that I don't intend to go into this area, I can't control, you know, everything the witness says or what comes up sometimes in examination, he would like to hear so that he has the context if anything arises on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll let the ruling stand as it is then. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, sir, could you first tell us what your date of birth is?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Sarajevo Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in what country could you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when did you come to reside in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: In July 1967, actually June 5, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And approximately how old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Ten year old.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is your current country of citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The United States of America. I also have citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I inherited from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how long have you been a US citizen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Since 1973.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you able to communicate in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, although frankly English is more of my language of personal and professional use.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your educational background is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. I have a bachelor of arts from Tulane University, summa cum laude. I have a law degree that is a doctor of jurisprudence from Tulane University. I have a master of business from Columbia University in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated you have a law degree, were you ever called to the bar?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you ever practice as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Very briefly. Most of my professional practice was as an investment banker.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how long did you work in that field, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I worked as an attorney for approximately four to five years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And sorry --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Most of that was as --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Most of that practice was as counsel to Standard & Poor's Corporation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You had mentioned a career in investment banking, and what year did you have that career start in and how long did you do that for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I moved over from counsel to Standard & Poor's to the business side of the company in 1983, 1984, and I continued to practice until in fact 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was your career change in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I was expecting it to be only a momentary diversion, but I was asked to become the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who approached you and asked to you assume that post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic, then chair of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where were you living at the time that you were approached to take that post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: New York, in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where were you going to be posted if you assumed the job of ambassador to the United Nations for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was New York, United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How long did you hold the post of ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: From 1992 until the end of 2000. Actually from May 22nd, 1992, when Bosnia was admitted to the United Nations, in the meantime, of course, I held several other positions on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you told us the date you took the post being May 22nd, 1992. And my question was how long did you hold the post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That would amount to almost nine years or over eight and a half years. I guess I should highlight that at that time I also in fact, at least for a short time, continued my private professional work as an investment banker. I was assuming that I was holding that post really for only a short duration until the war ended. Clearly it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. You told me or you told us that you were approached by President Izetbegovic, and can you tell me, did you have any diplomatic experience prior to being approached by the president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. Obviously my experience as an attorney and one involved in negotiations and investment banking was probably the most pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you assumed the post in May 1992, could you tell me did you have any staff or were you the only person working as a representative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina at the UN?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Actually, Bosnia's first mission was my business office, and therefore the only staff and the only assets that I had were those personal to me or to my partners in my business profession. Over time, of course, that evolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell me when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent country by the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That was in April of 1992. If I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were any other or did any other countries recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. Countries recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina one by one. Either on the basis of being approached by us, as was usually the case later on when I was the representative of the United Nations, or in fact they did it before Bosnia was admitted to the United Nations. Most of the early recognition came from what we refer to as the western European countries and United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you should have in front of you, I hope, a series of binders, and perhaps the Registrar can assist you with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you before you go to the binders. Can you tell us when Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted to the United Nations, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was May 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, this is Peter Guirguis, and I beg your forgiveness, Ms. Bolton, but I just wanted to alert the court to the fact that co-counsel for Mr. Sacirbey, Annemarie Corominas, has joined me here in the room. She's also familiar with the court's ruling and the court's rules with respect to the limitations of our discussions with Mr. Sacirbey. Just wanted to make the court aware of that before we proceeded. She just entered the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: My apologies to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your apology, Mr. Guirguis, but is there a need for both of you to be in there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Ms. Corominas is more familiar with the background of Mr. Sacirbey's case and she's travelled here today from the Philippines to be here with Mr. Sacirbey as well, and I would ask the court to allow her to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I hear any submissions. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the entire time that I've been practicing before this Tribunal, I've seen many witnesses come who would like the benefit of some support. Some of the witnesses who I've seen come who would like the benefit of some support, also in need of the benefit of legal support. I have yet to see ever - this is the first time that I've ever seen - a witness who is lawyer, and I think that the Chamber will find soon - a seasoned -- a diplomat well versed in the ways of a sophisticated give and take of questions and answers, and well versed in what I would call the conflicts that exist during verbal trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To have such support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I don't think the qualifications of the witness have to do -- have anything to do with whether or not that witness is entitled to a lawyer. We are now dealing here with just the question of the extra lawyer that is now coming into the room. How --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I object. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously, it's an unusual situation for the Prosecution because I don't know much about the allegations that are out there. There is obviously an issue of client/solicitor privilege that attaches to those issues, and I don't know also very much about the background of the two counsel. I know that the issues that are outstanding relate to both criminal matters and extradition matters, and I don't know whether they have different areas of expertise or different backgrounds. So I'm not really in a position to tell you very much. I think probably Mr. Guirguis and Ms. Corominas are better placed to explain why there is a need for both of them to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think that it's necessary for them to explain because they actually have no right of audience before this Tribunal. The only thing is they can only answer questions that are put to them if there are any questions put to them, and I do not intend to prolong this process. I think, Mr. Guirguis, I understand what you are saying, if it is possible for your colleague to listen from another place, it would be appreciative if she could do that because we are having quite a bit of problems here. I think one of you is enough in the room where the witness is testifying from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can change places at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps -- with the Court's permission, could we at least have the opportunity to switch positions in the courtroom here if a different issue arises, because as Ms. Bolton actually suggested and as I should have suggested to Your Honour, Ms. Corominas's expertise and background with Mr. Sacirbey's case does relate more to his extradition issues. And so if any of those issues come up, then I think she would be the one better placed in the room. So I'll start in the room now with her, and if it seems appropriate, then we'll switch out if Your Honour's ruling is that only one of us is permitted at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At that time if you can raise the issue with the Court, and then we'll decide it the time. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just place on the record that the Chamber has had redacted a portion read by Mr. Guy-Smith which related to an issue of the 18th of May, 2009, in which the Chamber says -- that's from page 5, lines 10 to 22, that's where the redaction is, because apparently something confidential is contained in there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my understanding. We received a note and we sent something back quite quickly saying we agreed. One, and I truly do hate to belabour the issue, but I overheard -- first of all, I see the witness speaking with his attorney which not supposed to occur at all. And second of all, I overheard the attorney indicating to the -- I'm sorry, I missed her name, the co-counsel that they have a -- have a method of listening to the proceedings outside of the room. Therefore, much of what has been said thus far and has been represented thus far, with regard to this particular attorney being present, that's Mr. Guirguis, I think is quite frankly disingenuous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear that and I don't know whether you want us to go into a trial within a trial about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I absolutely don't, Your Honour. I actually want to try the case that we have before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We were referring -- about to refer to a binder, sir, which should contain documents --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- from 1992, I believe is how they are labelled?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please turn to the first tab where you should find a document 65 ter 4999?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And it should be Resolution 755?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what did that resolution accomplish?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: This resolution was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think before the witness begins to give his opinion as what resolutions accomplish, there needs to be a further foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you read witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if he is going to be reading --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if he's going to be reading the resolutions, that's surely a waste of our time here. The Chamber can read the resolution. We don't need a witness reading resolutions to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's nothing inappropriate with the question, Your Honour. He's already, in fact, been asked and answered on what date the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations. I am now asking him to look at a document and identify what that document was and place that document in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can just sort of ask the questions that lay some kind of foundation for the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, as a result of your of your work as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations, did you have occasion to attend meetings of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And are you familiar, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I'm sorry to do this to you. I know you are -- the Registrar has just told me that the Registrar in New York has just communicated to her that he confirms that the counsel outside the room cannot hear what is taking place inside the room, as confirmation from the Registrar from New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sorry Your Honour, I didn't hear the last thing you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sacirbey, we were talking about your role as ambassador to the United Nations and whether you attended meetings of the Security Council, and in that capacity were you present when resolutions were passed with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the resolutions that were passed with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the document that's before you, sir, Resolution 755?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what did that accomplish?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That resolution in fact was an endorsement, a recommendation one would say, where the Security Council forwards to the General Assembly the recommendation that Bosnia-Herzegovina be admitted to the United Nations as a full member with all the rights and obligations. I would just like to caution that when this resolution was passed, I was not yet the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that would only happen a couple of days later, but I did have access at that time to Security Council members and of course to at least some of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wonder if this document to be entered as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us when the Republic of Slovenia Bosnian became a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was on the same date, May 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you turn to the next document in the tab that you have open, and it should be 65 ter 4998.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I am there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment, sir. Yes, sir. Sir, and can you confirm for us what this resolution accomplished?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: This is the same context as in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, this is for the Republic of Croatia, a recommendation that it be admitted as a member with full rights and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And we are looking at Resolution 753; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And Resolution 754 which is on the same page, what did it accomplish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we go to that one, I thought your questions, Madam Bolton, related to the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It did, sir, and the next question I think is going to clarify what the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what you were talk about previously, you were talking about Slovenia, and he said it was a resolution about Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, he has -- if I could ask the Court to scroll to Resolution 754, which is on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We got a little out of order there, sir, Resolution 754, what did it accomplish?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was the same as in the context of the Republic of Croatia and Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a recommendation by the Security Council for the United Nations General assembly to admit Slovenia as a full member with all the rights and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And looking at the document --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The three countries were -- the three countries were admitted at exactly the same time during the same proceedings in the General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I just notice that the date on this resolution is actually the 18th of May, 1992, and you've told us the actual date of admission is the 22nd May, 1992. Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. These are recommendations of the Security Council which then are left up to the General Assembly to in fact proceed, and number one, of course, have a vote, and second to actually through the proper proceedings admit these three states. So, in fact, the Security Council may take up this matter, this recommendation, at a separate time from the General Assembly, and in fact may take up the issue in each country individually and separately as it deems appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If that document can be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, May it please be given an exhibit number. Now, which document is this, ma'am? I know it's 4998, but is it Resolution 754, 753, or both.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's both, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before we go on to consider some other documents, sir, I just want to discuss a little bit about the United Nations itself and particularly the General Assembly and the Security Council which we've already been referring to here today. What -- can you tell me what the work is or what the General Assembly's jurisdiction is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The General Assembly of course consists of all the member states, and it addresses issues of general concern. It also has several other sub-bodies associated with it, that is various committees, agencies, institutions, if you would, these bodies may even in fact recommend to the Security Council, but generally the resolutions of the General Assembly do not have the same power; i.e., Chapter 7 or Chapter 6 power that the Security Council resolutions do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you are talking about power, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm really talking about mandatory performance under the chapters of the Chapter 7, for example, of the Security Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not believe that the witness has been called as an expert to interpret the various provisions of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but this question was not put to him, he volunteered this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we need to be very careful here because the manner in which the question was put was put in terms of jurisdiction, and with regard to the issue of jurisdiction, specifically because it is - as we all know - a legal term of art, I think we need to be stepping carefully, and I understand the Chamber's view with regard to issues concerning answers that come from witnesses as to whether or not they can be stricken or they can be limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the other concern here is that you stand up at a time when the witness is answering, not at the time when the question has been put.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, so the impression you are leaving me is that you are objecting to the answer, not to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm objecting to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least if you object to the question, if you could please stand up at the time the question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not in the middle of an answer by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For purposes of this objection, I think I must allow this to -- just finish off that point that you are raising, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if you could clarify what you meant when you were talking about -- you started to answer and to talk about mandatory compliance versus and then you were cut off, what were you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. The United Nations Security Council has unique authority in an actual context, which is to address great threats to peace and security, and in this context it can apply what's called Chapter 7 or Chapter 6 authority. Chapter 7 has the full weight of the international community behind it. And in fact, it is not only compulsory, but various methods may be applied to ensure compliance with such resolutions. Clearly, when we speak of chapter -- when we speak of UN Security Council versus General Assembly, the General Assembly is more, one would say, of a body that advises, that takes stands on international issues, while in fact this UN Security Council, in fact, is one that can impose measures including mandatory measures, including potentially forced sanctions, things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just going back to the General Assembly, sir, when it meets are its meetings held in public or in private?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They are always in public.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about the Security Council when it meets?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The UN Security Council may meet in private consultations. In fact, there's a special room on the side of the Security Council Chamber for such consultations. As far as I am aware of, all the votes of the Security Council, though, are taken in public, and such debates associated with those votes are in public. And UN Security Council members do have a history of meeting also in partial membership, that is two, three, five members may meet to discuss these issues beyond any sort of formal setting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How many members are there on the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: As of today it's 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How many of those seats of the 15 -- are any of those seats of the 15 permanent seats that don't change?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Five are permanent members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the other ten then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The other ten rotate in two year terms. Actually five and five, so there are elections every year for five members, and those non-permanent members stay on the council for a period of two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And during the time of the Bosnian war in 1992 to 1995, were any of the parties to the conflict Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they -- either of them have a seat in the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, not until not -- well, until the late 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia have a seat in the Security Council during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've mentioned that this Security Council can meet in private and you indicated that the number of members who would attend those sessions would vary. If you weren't a member of the Security Council, and by that I mean you don't have a seat on the Security Council, could you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: You may be called upon by some of those countries to consult. Bosnia and Herzegovina was frequently called upon by some of those countries to provide insight. Sometimes to relay information to other Security Council members through those meetings. We frequently met with what was then called a non-align group. Sometimes we met with what were -- what was called the P3, P4, P5, or P3 plus 2. For example the P3 plus 2 was a reference to the two permanent EU member, the United States, and generally there were two other EU members that were non-permanent on the council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there, sir. With respect to the public meetings of the Security Council that you have alluded to, if you didn't have a seat in the Security Council, could you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. If the meeting what a formal meeting, you would actually sit on the side of the Chambers, and each county does actually have a seat designated for it to the extent that there were informal consultations going on in the anti-Chamber, if you would, most of us were not only aware of it but we made sure we were present, and we were present in what's called the Security Council delegates lounge where in facts we exchanged views, provided information, or whatever was appropriate in that diplomatic context.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm only interested right now, sir, on -- in your ability to participate in the public sessions and be present in the public sessions. So you've told us, I think, that you could be present in those sessions; is that correct, the public sessions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you entitled to participate in the discussions as right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, we would have to make an application to participate. That application did not have to be granted, and that application could be limited to the ability to sit at the table and observe, that is as one that is considered a party to the issue, or in fact you could participate with the right to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And would you ever have a right to vote in the Security Council as a member state that didn't have a seat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, you would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I see the time Your Honour did you want to take the break at the regular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed we would. We'll take the break and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, does the admonition stand with regard to no contact between the witness and the lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The admonition stand with regard to the issue of no contact between the witness and his lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether we can still find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: I'm here, Your Honour, and I understand the admonition not to discuss any substance of the witness's testimony with him over the course of the entire week absent any issues that arise with respect to incrimination or things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: The rule is well understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are so warned. May we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue, the clerk pointed out to me during the break that the first exhibit that was marked today, being Exhibit P2428, actually contains two resolutions, Resolution 755, that we discussed, and there's another resolution, 763, and I'll just clarify for the record that the Prosecution isn't relying on Resolution 763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, before the break, we were talking about your work at the United Nations, and we briefly touched on the fact that when you first became the ambassador, that you were basically working out of your home and so forth. Was there ever a time when there was anyone other than yourself working for the mission on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we touch now on the status of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the United Nations during this time-period. And I want to start by asking if the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we've already established that when it began to break up that Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as Slovenia applied for and were granted membership in the United Nations. Can you tell me whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we go any further the question is as it's presently put forth, which is "when it began to break up," is historically inaccurate to the extent that it's going to be of any issues to the Chamber. The question should be properly framed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't think, Your Honour, that there's any issue with respect in these proceedings. My friend's objection to the use of "break up," it doesn't have any connotation. I can reword the question if you would like, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you like to reword, reword it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Slovenia declared themselves independent, after that process, sir, can you tell me whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia followed suit and applied for membership at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, it did not. Not at least during the period of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was its -- what was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's position on membership -- its entitlement to membership at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at this point unless there's a foundation laid, I would object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Foundation for what, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's position with regard to its entitlement to its membership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what kind of foundation should be laid for that kind of question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there is as a matter of fact a series of legal documents to discuss this matter and was a hotly contested legal issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. Are you discussing legalities or are you discussing time-frames, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm not discussing the legalities, I'm trying to discuss what its status was at the United Nations, what rights it had, and my friend is right that there is some documents but I can't -- I'm trying to introduce into evidence those documents so that we can have clarification as to what its status was. I'm not asking for a legal question at all, I'm just asking for the historical context, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think if you can tie to your question a time-frame, it will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In -- let's look at the spring of 1992, Mr. Sacirbey, could you tell me what position the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taking with respect to membership for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was a fluid situation. Certainly the -- many of the diplomats that were once representing the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did in fact continue to represent the Serbia Montenegro. Others, in fact, resigned from those posts and went on either into private life or into representing other countries. It was, though, quite clear that there was a continuity of the presence of some of these diplomats, although not until the September of 1992 was the status of Serbia Montenegro, that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, addressed by the United Nations General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to September of 1992, could you tell us if there was any discussion in the Security Council on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Certainly at that period of time immediately before September, but throughout the time, and the question was did in fact the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia Montenegro, have the right of continuity to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: If Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Well, a continuity -- let me give you another example. Russia was assumed to have continuity for the Soviet Union, but in fact in the case of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not assumed, and there was no agreement regarding its continuity, and in fact Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and other states subsequently did challenge that continuity, that is that in fact Serbian Montenegro, that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, would need to make its own application to become a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about continuity, can you just clarify what you mean, continuity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: State continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, once again if we are talking about this from a standpoint of a legal standpoint, there has been no foundation laid for this gentleman to discuss the matter. If we are talking about it from another standpoint, then I don't object to the question but since the question as phrased is sufficiently vague and there are legal issues with regard to all of these terms that are of importance to the Trial Chamber's consideration, I would request that the questions framed are quite specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question to be from a legal standpoint, and I thought it was sufficiently specific and clearly excluding the legalities, it was just asking what this witness knows as a person who was in United Nations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you explain what you are talking about when you are talking about continuity with respect to membership in the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We were talking about state or legal continuity which means that in fact the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro, would not need to make an application to become a member as in fact Russia did not in the case of the break-up of the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case in fact it was the -- a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the answer given by the witness indicates the exact problem that I raised, specifically -- especially after your particular ruling in which the witness said "We were talking about state or legal continuity..." right after you had indicated in your understanding that the question was not to be from a legal standpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, my understanding is that this witness is a fact witness, he's not an expert. And I'm -- he's telling us what he understands the facts to have been, and whether those facts were legal or not legal, we will hear evidence on as to when the legal succession took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you may -- as a matter of fact you may or you may not, Your Honour, and with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if we don't then it's not a hotly disputed issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that this witness is rendering opinions that deal with legal matters predicated upon his understanding of legal matters, it is of some moment. But if we are going to be in a situation where we are going to have expert evidence, for example, on Article 6 and Article 7, if we are going to be going through an entire discussion of how the United Nations is put together and how these specific provisions apply to member states or non-member states, and the Prosecution is intending on doing such things, fine. But in the absence of that, which you have, is you have a gentleman who is giving legal opinion about -- in areas where he has not been yet established as any expert and as you yourself said. He has been called as a fact witness not as a legal witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but the thing is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- I haven't heard him giving -- opining. I've heard him tell us what he knows from what he observed when he was there. He hasn't given opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he used specifically the terminology that you had but a moment before indicated was not the thrust of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. The -- and my friend can object to my questions, but he continues to object to the witness's answers, and these are matters he can deal with in cross-examination rather than continually interrupt my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand Ms. Bolton's position, however, there's a problem here. And I understand the court's ruling with regard to the -- its view that witness's answer that is non-responsive or goes far afield from the question is not something that can be objected to. I happen to take issue with that and don't believe that should be the state of the law but that is what you have ruled. This is not helpful, however, to the Chamber. This is not helpful at all because if you have a witness who is engaged in giving you non-responsive answers, and going far afield from the issue at hand, we are engaged in a couple of things: One is a wasting of time; two is a witness who is being, in fact, utilized in a manner for which they're not called. He is being utilized as an expert when he is a fact witness, and there's slippage, and the slippage is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the extent you comment on my ruling, I just want to say to you, sir, that that ruling stands that I made earlier. And whether you take issue with it or not it's another matter. You can decide what you want to do about that. And I just want to say to you, if anything comes from the witness that is not -- that is far afield from issues before Court, the proper basis is relevance. And, unfortunately, yes, I still say, it is not in my knowledge permissible to object to a witness's answer because then otherwise you might as well take the stand and answer on behalf of the witness. If the witness has been asked a question and he answers the way he answers, that's how he answers. You can object to a question, and I stand by that ruling, and what you want to do with that is your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand you in that regard. There's common objection in American jurisprudence called objection, none responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. We are not in American jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But to the extent you have a witness who is going far afield, we need to have some remedy, perhaps the remedy is for the Court to instruct the witness to answer the question asked as opposed to going off on a lark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Relevance becomes the basis of objections. If anybody goes far afield, the question becomes relevance, not none responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I'm clear with regard to the Court's position: If a witness gives an answer which I deem to be not relevant, am I in a position to object to that answer on the grounds of relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'd have to object to the question that's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying if the question is a relevant question but the answer is an irrelevant answer, is the Court's ruling that I can object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I understand the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- then I -- then I understand the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Bolton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, in the binder before you, perhaps to clarify this issue, I could ask you to turn to the next document, which is tab 2, Resolution 757 which is Prosecution Exhibit 202 in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Thank you, we are getting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I have that in front of me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could turn to the second page of the resolution. There is a paragraph that starts with the underlined word "noting" approximately halfway down the page. Are you able to locate that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The text says: "Noting that the claim by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro to continue automatically the membership of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the United Nations has not been generally accepted." Does this document, sir, accurately reflect the position the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taking on this issue in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It reflects, of course, the view of the United Nations that it was not generally accepted. On the other hand, of course the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was contending that it may have had or did have automatic membership.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. You've alluded to the fact, sir, that there was eventually in September 1992 a ruling of sorts on this issue or clarification in the Security Council, and I wonder go you could please turn to the second document in that same tab. It is Defence Exhibit 30 in these proceedings. Resolution 777.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's correct. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this the document you were referring to in your previous testimony, sir, or were you referring to some other document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, this is the recommendation of the Security Council to the General Assembly upon which the General Assembly did eventually act.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the General Assembly agree with the recommendation or disagree with the recommend?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It, in fact, did agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: As a result of that ruling, could you tell me what rights the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had in the General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It did not have the right to be seated or to participate in the actual work of the General Assembly. Obviously did not have the right to vote. Although, in fact, there was a plaque left in the General Assembly reflecting the Federal Republic -- or actually the name Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you talk about participate in the actual work of the General Assembly, would that include participating in discussions in the General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When the General Assembly and the Security Council were, for example, considering passing resolutions, was there any information that would be circulated about those draft resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: There would be. Usually before the resolution was adopted, there at least would be a draft resolution that would be circulated and of course once it was adopted then it no longer would be a draft.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did the General Assembly and the Security Council circulate other kinds of documents to member states?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They did. They may have been reports from the Secretary-General's office, that is the Secretariat. It may have been documents from other institutions or agencies of the United Nations, rapporteurs, and of course of member states.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what were the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's rights to receive those kind of documents?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all, we do know that they did receive those documents, and second of all, we do know that they in fact did also circulate documents at least subsequent to this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the reason you say you know they received those kinds of documents is what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Because we had firsthand knowledge. In part because we really were quite focused on the issue of what was the status of Serbian Montenegro and to what extent they in fact did have certain rights of membership while maybe not having all the rights of membership. They certainly did have diplomats accredited to the United Nations, visas were issued, documents were distributed and received. Even at some point in time they participated in the discussions of the Security Council upon their request.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were their rights of participation in the Security Council any different than the rights enjoyed by Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's a little bit difficult to say because we as a member state had the right to ask to be seated and to participate. Serbian Montenegro also did subsequently make the same request and at some point in time in fact they were granted. Whether it was perceived by the Security Council members and others to be exactly the same right or not is difficult to say, but from a perspective of actually being there, receiving documents, being part of the discussion, it was very much similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who was -- you mentioned the fact that there had been a representative of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the United Nations. Do you remember what that person's name was in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I don't remember his full name to be very honest with you, I only had one interaction with him and he actually left before we became -- that is before Bosnia-Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Who became the FRY representative at the -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia representative at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The time-frames are interesting in a sense that there was, of course, what would he call a Charge d'affair at one time. Then there was Ambassador Dzokic and Ambassador Jovanovic who were there most of the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how do you spell Ambassador Jokic's name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It's -- well, in --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: In our language it would -- yes, I guess that would be J-o-k-i-c-h. But the spelling would be quite different in the Bosnian Croat or Serba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what would that spelling be in Bosnian and Croatian spelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be different. It's actually -- D-z --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you spell it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, D-z-o-k-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's little thing at the end of the C that indicates it's a CH sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Dealing with Ambassador Dzokic, did he have any staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, he did. In fact, the staff was there, I believe, before he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Approximately how large was his staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Again, during this period of time there were probably anywhere from ten to as many as 20 plus staff. Now, how many of them were accredited diplomats, probably it was more like 5 to 10, again depending on the time-frame. Usually, also countries would tend to bring in more staff when there were particular issues of great interest or, for example, during the General Assembly session in the fall, countries would tend to bring in temporary diplomatic staff to address the greater workload.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had a military attache at any time from May of 1992 to the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm actually not certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell me how much contact you or your staff had with Mr. Dzokic on a day-to-day basis or weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: There was actually pretty extensive contact. I personally refrained from direct contact because the fact that Serbian Montenegro did not provide Bosnia-Herzegovina with diplomatic recognition. I did not wish, therefore, to reciprocate with any legitimacy. It was in fact a diplomatic option. But there was certainly interaction and it was not one of those combative situations, but because again of the diplomatic situation we did not interact that frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would your staff share with you what happened in those interactions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I would encourage them to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could the speakers please make pauses before question and answer for benefit of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, Mr. Interpreter. Yes, Madam Bolton, and you, Mr. Sacirbey, both of you are speaking in English and we are having interpretation into various other languages. If you could please have a pause between question and answer to allow for the interpretation to flow smoothly. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we might get a time-frame or some specificity with regard to the interaction between these two parties, that would be of some assistance, as opposed to the general and rather ambiguous state of the record as it stands right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am talking -- sir, just for clarification of my last series of questions, I'm talking about the entire time-period from May of 1992 to the end of 1995. That's what I intended when I asked the question of how many contact you or your staff were having, and if -- could you please clarify if there were time periods where there was more or less contact than you've already indicated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The contact probably was more frequent toward the end of that period or at least the middle of it. In parts, because of course the staff that I had evolved into significantly more, in part because an exchange of information sometimes was in fact necessary. Nonetheless, the exchange was continuous during that time-frame. There were many diplomats eventually that we brought on on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina that knew some of the diplomats of Serbian Montenegro personally and interacted with them quite more regularly than I would, and including my deputy at that time Ivan Misic, and they in fact did fill me in on those discussions or those talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And based on the information you were receiving from your staff, could you comment on how well informed Mr. Dzokic appeared to be on the events that were transpiring in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object on a couple of grounds. It calls for speculation based upon multiple unsourced hearsay, except to the extent that we've had the name of one individual who was his deputy staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of your staff, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. During that time-frame it was quite extensive, so let me make sure that I'm as complete as I can be. But I doubt if I'm going to get everyone in there. There was Miles Raguz, there was Ivan Misic, Nenad Periskic, Amela Sapcanin, those were my immediate diplomatic staff. I'm sure I'm leaving several others. Michael Young [phoen]. Phil Colin [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is that your list, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm sure I'm leaving some people out. At any point in time we had probably at least five accredited diplomats starting, let's say, with the fall of 1992. That number was rather fluid and the personalities were fluid. Many of them were volunteers, and they were many times employed to be addressing the specific United Nations committees, for example the 3rd committee or the 1st committee so that in fact Bosnia-Herzegovina could be active in all the work of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And you've talked about diplomatic staff specifically. Who would have actually had contact with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Actually, most frequently would have been either Ivan Misic or Miles Raguz or Amela Sapcanin or John Kraljic [phoen] which is a name I'm adding just now. Or Phil Colin, I think -- I think those were the ones that would have been more frequently involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So based on the reports that you received back from those five individuals as to their discussions with Mr. Dzokic, could you comment on how well informed Mr. Dzokic appeared to be? THE COURT: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, the question as posed mis-characterizes the witness's answer, so I'll start with that. And we'll go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the alleged mischaracterization is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Question asked on page 40, line 6 through 8 deals with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Staff. That would be multiple individuals, none of whom have been named. Question at page 40, lines 13 through 15 deal with specifically as to their discussions with Mr. Dzokic, but that's not the state of our record. The state of our record is that he was discussing who his staff talked to with regard to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's staff, not with Mr. Dzokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So I'm trying to locate the record, Your Honour. My initial question which had to do -- that my friend objected to which had to do with the fact that he received reports from his staff, and then we talked about the fact that there were five individuals basically who had contact with the FRY diplomatic mission, and in my position, with respect, Your Honour, is that when you combine those two statements, it's clear that we are talking about the same individuals as being individuals who reported their contacts with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's an entirely different position than whether or not anybody spoke to Mr. Dzokic, and she's identified the question with regard to Mr. Dzokic. Now, whether or not the identified individuals of Mr. Sacirbey's staff spoke with individuals in the FRY staff is something that I believe probably happened. Who those individuals were I have no way of knowing because there's no information about that, but more importantly what she has done is she's taken a collective hearsay grouping of individuals on both sides and then refined it to Mr. Dzokic which is inappropriate because that's not what the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Actually, my initial question at page 37, lines 18 to 19 was specific to contact with Mr. Dzokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think Ms. Bolton misses the point, because if she takes a look at page 39, beginning at line -- I think it's line 5 through the end of that particular section is where this -- we went off on this particular unfortunate journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I understood you to be asking two different questions. You asked about contact with staff and then you asked when the -- your opposite number objected, it was when you asked him about reports from Mr. Dzokic, from discussions with Mr. Dzokic. Maybe just so that we can run a little bit smoothly, if you could just focus your question if you want to talk about reports, and I suspect when you talk of reports you're talking of official reports between specifically Mr. Dzokic and any of the staff of the BiH embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When I use the term "report" I'll clarify with the witness, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- if Your Honour is confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could, please. I guess I seem to sense that Mr. Guy-Smith's problem is he doesn't know -- want a mixture of hearsay of evidence from unknown sources to specific information coming from specific people to specific people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, my question, Mr. Sacirbey, if we could go back to the beginning is, did your -- you've given us the name of five diplomatic staff. Can you tell me how much contact on a day-to-day basis during the conflict those individuals would have had with Mr. Dzokic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm quite certain that at least one of them, which is my deputy at that time Ivan Misic, had quite regular contact with Mr. Dzokic. I would also add that frequently when we were dealing with diplomats from other states, we were not necessarily dealing with them on a first name basis. The references in the United Nations generally are to people as the country that they represent. It is quite common in the United Nations that you are not always dealing with people whose first or last name you would know. But with Mr. Dzokic, I remember very clearly that Mr. Misic frequently gave me the updates of his discussions with Mr. Dzokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And when gave you updates and reported what he discussed with Mr. Dzokic, could you tell me how well informed Mr. Dzokic appeared to be, based on those reports, as to events that were transpiring in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
