utterances.text: I was left with the strong impression that the information was extensive and in many cases detailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, what do you mean when you say that the information was extensive and in many cases detailed? My question was how well informed Mr. Dzokic appeared to be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: He seemed to be well informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What kind of issues would your representatives discuss with Mr. Dzokic or members of his staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Frequently they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, if we could have some time-frame with regard to this apart from a three year time-frame. There are many many things that happened during those three years, and they have different legal as well as factual import to the matters before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was under the impression that I was running my examination-in-chief and my friend may want to clarify in cross-examination issues such as this, but it's not a proper objection to a question that doesn't -- that it's not specific enough to suit counsel's needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's vague as to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've been given a time-frame of 1992 to 1995. If you're unable to hone in on a shorter time, fine. If you are not, that's the time we have got to live with and Mr. Guy-Smith can clarify things in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sacirbey, if you could answer my question about the kinds of issues that were discussed and during that time-frame 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, the importance of this is that we do have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to make pauses before question and answer for the benefit of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you heard what the interpreter said. Mr. Guy-Smith, you can start your -- what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I might, we do have an indictment here and the indictment period is discrete and does not cover the entire period of time that Ms. Bolton's question discusses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, how I now understand Mr. Guy-Smith is -- you are going outside the time-frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, there's already been, I think, Your Honour, a series of rulings in this case that indicate that matters precede the indictment period may still be relevant in terms of issues such as foreseeability. What I'm trying to establish at this point in time, Your Honour, the relevance is the flow of communication, the knowledge of the federal -- the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It's relevant that they knew of events, for example, in 1993, and I appreciate that there will be a separate issue to be argued as to the extent to which General Perisic was updated on any information that was available, but I think it's still relevant that the FRY representatives knew what was going on -- sorry, the diplomatic representatives knew what was going on in 1992, 1993, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection would be overruled then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey, if we could go back then. We were talking about generalities here of the time-period of 1992 to 1995, and if you could just highlight for us what kind of issues were typically discussed with the FRY mission by your representatives?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Certainly the primary issue we would try to bring to their attention are the reports of various atrocities, actions, military actions within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of course the implications for the population as well as the country. The FRY may also wish to discuss the issue of sanctions. Within that context we may also ask the transport of military goods and other goods or people that may in fact come from Serbian Montenegro into Bosnia-Herzegovina. We may discuss, in fact, the status of Serbian Montenegro at the United Nations. We may discuss, depending on the moment, the various reports issued by the Secretary-General reporting on the condition of the population on the military actions, where those military actions may have come from, and of course the consequences for the humanitarian situation, things like delivery of food and medicines. I'm sure I can go on for quite sometime, but I hope that serves the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you use the word "we may discuss," are you indicating that these issues were or were not discussed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, they were. Again, of course, keeping in mind the time-frame, all of these issues were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Tell me, was there ever a time between May 1992 and the 24th day of November, 1998, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not represented at the United Nations in New York?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that there were times when the Bosnian war was the subject of discussions in the General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. We, in fact, initiated such a discussion as early as the fall of -- actually late summer fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were there occasions when the Bosnian war was also the subjects of discussions at the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That was very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, were there ever occasions when the subject of the Bosnian war was being discussed in either of those forums when someone from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's mission was not present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I cannot recall such a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there any occasions between May of 1992 and the end of 1995 when you were permitted to address the Security Council on matters relating to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the occasions that you spoke, could you tell us how frequently or infrequently someone from the FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was present, and by that I mean a member of their mission?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were always present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the context of having discussions at the General Assembly and the Security Council at the United Nations, would I be correct in assuming that there had to have been some efforts for the Security Council and General Assembly to keep abreast of what was happening in the region?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What sources of information did the Security Council have available to it in terms of what was actually happening in the region?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all, they may have had various reports from the Secretariat, that is UN representative agencies. Whether it was UNPROFOR or such other missions, rapporteurs, as those were institutions directly associated with the United Nations, and there were multiple such institutions. They may have also received reports from other international institutions, for example, the EU monitoring mission. They may have received reports from related institutions, for example, various groupings of states, and of course, they would receive information from member states themselves, and those member states might in fact also include media reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you've used the word "may" again, does that mean they did or did not have information available from the sources you've listed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: In fact in all of those instances were reflected at least on several occasions in actual sources. I do know that, of course, even Bosnia-Herzegovina, in my capacity as ambassador, did at times convey to the Security Council media reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that information was available from UNPROFOR at times, and I wonder if I could ask you to turn to tab 15A in the binder that's before you. And this is 65 ter number 5986.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We are having just a little bit of difficulty identifying the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It should be tab 15A.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was just in a separate book, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, it should be in that -- oh, yes, sorry, you have the Bosnian translations, you are correct. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Okay. And what is the number --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am sorry, it's 65 ter 5986, and the title at the top of the document should be "UNPROFOR Press and Information Press Release, 16 March, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My question is with respect to the release of information from UNPROFOR, how often did they release press releases such as this one during the time-period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was frequent but by no means comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know what you mean by comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The information was released very frequently, but it does not mean that in fact every and any information was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would the information that the Security Council be the same as the information that was released to the press?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We have been -- we know that there were some confidential briefings that were given to the Security Council as a whole, but more likely at least to some Security Council members. But by and large, most of the information that was available to the Security Council was eventually available to all member states, to others that were part of the diplomatic staff, and of course the media. Q.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that document, Your Honour, could be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2430.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In your capacity as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have access to any sources of information that wouldn't have been available to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there ever occasions when you came into possession of information that you wanted to place in front of the Security Council or make them aware of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How would you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Well, as we just discussed, once a document was made a document of the General Assembly or the Security Council, then in fact it was available to all, and it was quote unquote a public document. So to the extent that we in fact would received information from any source that we believe was credible, we would then submit it to either to the Secretary-General's office or more likely to the president of the Security Council or in some instances it may have been also made a document to the General Assembly. Regardless, when we requested that it be distributed as a document of those bodies, of those institution, then in fact it would be a public document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in what form would you report the information?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: What we would do is we would attach a letter to one of these institutions, most of the times it was the president of the Security Council, asking that in fact that information be distributed as a document of the Security Council. At that point in time, again it would be a public document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, notwithstanding the issue of its status, receiving copies of your documents?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And in some instances we would actually make certain that those documents would be even directly mailed to the representatives of or and to other member states. So that in fact some of the documents may have even gone directly from our office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that some of the documents were mailed, how else do you know that they were in fact receiving copies of your correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Once in fact -- actually, I want to make sure I'm correct in my representation. Most of the times, at least during that time-frame, documents were either faxed to other countries, or they may have been hand delivered. But once a document was made a document of the United Nations Security Council or the other institution that I mentioned, then all member statements in fact would receive that, and we knew that in fact the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia/Serbian Montenegro was on the distribution list. Needless to say, these documents were sometimes discussed, they were part of those discussions that we mentioned before with representatives of Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Any reason to believe that representatives from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia mission read any of your letters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Simply because there was reply either in person or subsequent in some form of a formal response. I am not aware of any instance where those documents had caught anyone by surprise at the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is that somehow they did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What kinds of topics would you discuss in your correspondence, typically?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Most of the time they related, of course, again to the human situation on the ground. The abuse of the population, what we referred to at that time as genocide, and we still believe it. What we discussed as the humanitarian situation, the interruption of food and medicines. Frequently the supply of military goods and men coming from Serbian Montenegro, attacks initiated from across the border, violations of sanctions, violations of the border monitoring. And in some instances, of course, we may have relayed -- particular conditions may be related it to Bosnia-Herzegovinian citizens being held in the other neighbouring countries, particularly Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what were you -- sorry, would you be able to estimate or give us any idea of how many letters you might have written between 1992 and 1995 on the topics that you articulated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We were quite persistent. We of course tried to convey not only the specific deeds that were involved, but a systematic approach on the part of the forces of Serbian Montenegro and their agents in Bosnia. I would say we probably averaged a document more frequent than every other day. Let's say about 200 documents a year. Sometimes multiple documents during even a single day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What were you trying to achieve by writing that many letters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: In part each one of those events needed to be noted, particularly if there was something that was related to the human condition. I felt it was my obligation to take note of each victim, take note of each crime committed against the Bosnian people. I did not wish those victims to be forgotten. So that was my way of conveying some sort of respect to their individual identity. But also, it was important, I think, to convey that there was a systematic effort underway to not only undermine the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in fact to engage in great violations of international humanitarian law, that is genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who were you trying to convey that to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Of course, the international community as a whole. The member states. The media. And of course Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We began this discussion by talking about information that was available to the Security Council in making their decisions and you indicated that one of the sources of information were media reports. Can you tell us what kind of access to media resources such as television, radio, newspaper, delegates had at the UN headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We would have access of course to all of that through various channels, but we might also have access to more in the view of the fact that most media institutions, or at least a the larger ones are represented at the United Nations. There are various media reports that were also put out beyond the normal channels in what was called the UN correspondence association area on the third floor of UN headquarters. We may in fact have some of these media reports also sent out to us specifically by such reporters. On several occasions certainly I was contacted directly either to ask questions or more accurately, I guess, in response to your question, to convey certain pieces of information that might be relevant to the work of the United Nations Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You talked about there being a correspondence association area on the third floor of UN headquarters. Would you have to go up and get information or request information from them, or would they distribute it without asking, or what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all, at the time when I was present, and I believe that practice still continues, countries and sometimes media institutions will put out the reports in like a filer. And also of course sometimes those filers would be actually directly faxed or sent to all the member states. Most of the time that was employed by other member states, but at times it could be also employed by some of the media organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. One of the resources I was asking about was television. What access to television coverage was there at the UNHQ, UN Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: There was, of course, the United Nations TV which was something that was available to all -- well, let me rephrase that. It was available to in fact all of Manhattan on cable. And I know that my mission in fact did have access to that UN television channel. And then of course we would have access to all the other media, in particular CNN, BBC, the other major broadcast stations in the United States, ABC, CBS, NBC, at that time. And they --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you say you may have -- sorry. When you are talking about we had access, are you talking specifically about your mission? Or are you talking about this being available in public areas or something else entirely?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think I should be very specific. I know what I had available to my mission, and of course I could easily move the channels around. I know also that in several public areas of the United Nations including at the United Nations Security Council delegates area, there was a television set up. Most of the time it was broadcasting CNN.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that delegates area is the area you've already discussed as being by the Security Council anti-room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. It's the UN Security Council lounge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now start to deal with the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina chronologically, sir. And if we could -- if you could turn your mind back to May 1992, can you tell us what the situation was the time you assumed your post with respect to the ability of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to acquire arms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was deemed to be subject to an arms embargo imposed upon what at that time was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or actually the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab 5 in the binder that you previously had. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are going there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's 65 ter 6036.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were just talking about an arms embargo having been imposed on the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you look at this document and tell me if this is the document that you were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. And this document was referred to in subsequent resolutions. That's why I'm very familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could this document please be tendered as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2431, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that this arms embargo resolution was referred to in subsequent documents, and if you could turn to the next page in that same tab, you should see a document 65 ter 4997.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We are just having a little difficulty locating it, let me make sure. Resolution 740?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. And if you could look at chapter -- sorry, brief indulgence. Yes, on the first page you have before you there's paragraph that starts with the words underlined "expressing concern," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this one of the resolutions, then, that referred to Resolution 713?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. Although, I will note again that I was not the permanent representative of Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I take it you weren't present then when this resolution was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able it to say, sir, whether this text is a authentic copy of Resolution 740?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Again, because it was referred to by subsequent resolutions, I did review all of these during my tenure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could this be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At any point during May 1992 to the end of 1995, was there any discussion of lifting the arms embargo with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who initiated that discussion generally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Certainly Bosnia-Herzegovina did, but there were other states who felt that the situation was one where Serbian Montenegro was in fact fully armed while Bosnia-Herzegovina was left without the means to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and that in fact the arms embargo created an uneven situation where in fact contributed to the conflict rather than reduced it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ever take a position on the issue either orally or in writing, of whether -- and the issue I mean whether the arms embargo with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina should be lifted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was very clear in its preparations that the arms embargo should continue with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was any explanation offered as to why they were opposed to lifting the arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was the explanation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That, in fact, Bosnia was -- if Bosnia-Herzegovina, as they referred to us at that time Bosnian Muslims were given weapons that it would somehow increase the war, increase the fighting, and that in fact it would just only fuel the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Next document I'd like or development I'd like to discuss with you, sir, is Resolution 752 which we'll find at tab 6 of the binder. And this is already in evidence as Exhibit P201.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, my first question is, the date on this resolution is the 15th of May, 1992, which was before you officially became the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you tell us whether you were present when this resolution was debated and passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Actually, I was present because by then our admission to the United Nations was envisioned, and I was acted as an informal representative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we've already talked a bit about the fact that there was a transition period with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the change in delegates, can you recall whether there was anyone from Serbian Montenegro in attendance when this was discussed, or from the Socialist --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Or from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: At that time I believe the name was only used Yugoslavia, and, yes, there was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I do not. I do not remember the individual by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The resolution, looking at the first page of the document, it's divided obviously into paragraphs, and the third paragraph on the first page starts with the words "deeply concerned." Have you located that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm just -- yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It says: "Deeply concerned about the serious situation in certain parts of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in particular about the rapid and violent deterioration of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And I am going to go slower, I'm sorry. And then there is, if you would turn your attention to - brief indulgence - the second page, there are numbered paragraphs, there's a numbered paragraph 6, where there is a reference to: "the forcible expulsion of persons from the areas where they live and attempts to change the ethnic composition of the population." My question for you, sir, is could you tell us what events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was going on that prompted the inclusion of that language by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all, there were reports received from independent sources including UN sources, European sources, certain human rights groups and media. Also at that time with Dr. Haris Silajdzic, the foreign minister of Bosnia, we had started to provide our own information to the Secretary-General's office regarding the events. As well as to certain member states who in fact accorded us an opportunity to meet with them. And I remember this very vividly because one of the discussions was, Do we call these events genocide?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, sir, I've got to interrupt you because --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- we are going to need to take a break in a moment. But could you just answer the question which was, you know, what were the actual events before we discuss how they were or weren't going to be characterised.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were already events happening. In particular, we were out in the Drina river valley, several towns at that time were under attack. We knew that in fact individuals either had been murdered or forced out of their homes. We had seen refugees coming to other urban centres in the region, like Sarajevo or central Bosnia, and there were of course many refugees already pouring outside of the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we were trying as best as we could to accumulate these reports or rely upon other independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to this issue, but I think it's time for tour next break, sir. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, before the break you were talking about reports you were receiving from the Drina river valley, around the time that preceded or were part of the discussion of Resolution 752, and you talked about the fact that individuals were either being murdered or forced out of their homes. When you talk about individuals, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm referring to the non-Serb population, particularly the Bosniak or Bosnian Muslim population, but also any of those that in fact stood up the para-military as well as the regular military forces that at that time were occupying Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Apart from the reports from the Drina river valley, were you receiving reports from any other regions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, we were receiving some reports from the Krajina region, some reports from Herzegovina, which is the southwestern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of course Sarajevo. At that time Sarajevo had practically been encircled and was already under sniper fire and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm looking at again the text of Resolution 752, and I note that at numbered paragraph 3, that the Security Council included a demand that all forms of interference from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, including by units of the Yugoslavia People's Army as well as elements of the Croatian army, cease immediately. Can you tell me why there was reference to the Yugoslav People's Army or JNA are included in this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA was involved, if not always in actual campaigns of what was then called ethnic purification, then they in fact were involved in consolidating those position that were achieved through ethnic cleansing or purification, and in fact they were also involved in the siege of Sarajevo and several other towns. The JNA had been asked to leave by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact had not complied, and we viewed them as in fact not only a combat as an adversary to the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a further reference in this document, and I'm looking at the first page of the document, sixth paragraph from the top, paragraph starts with the words "having considered" and there is then a reference to an announcement made by Belgrade on the 4th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I note that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. What was the announcement that Belgrade made?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Under pressure Belgrade in fact was asked to withdraw from -- any of its military forces from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and in fact was supposed to comply under that provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, so the announcement from Belgrade then, was that to the effect that they would comply or not comply, or?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: As we understood it, it was one that they would comply. But there was, of course, some lack of commitment that we understood there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of information that was subsequently received in the wake of that announcement by your government, and by that I mean the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what did you understand was happening with respect to the -- to the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We received very little indication that actually withdrawal had been underway, and there were even indications to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: As far as your government was concerned, what was happening with the JNA troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Certainly it had been hoped at the beginning of the year that the JNA would at least be a neutral force, if not somehow providing some sense of nullifying the para-military force that had already become active. But at this time it was quite evident that the JNA was in fact undertaking military operations which were against the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, of course in particular, in many ways inflicting harm upon the population as well as besieging cities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, my question wasn't specific enough. When I referred to what was happening with the JNA, I meant to be specific to the issue of whether -- we were talking about whether it was withdrawn. What was your understanding as to what the JNA was doing in terms of the actual withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We had no indications of withdrawal, I certainly was not given indications and my government felt there that was no withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So if the troops weren't withdrawing, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They were staying put, actually in some cases digging in, and as I said we actually received some indications that even new troops and new materiel was coming across the Drina river, from Serbian Montenegro to be more precise. Some troops had also by the way come in from the other side, withdrawing JNA troops had come in from Croatia, presumably withdrawing through Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbian Montenegro but in fact had stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I should also emphasise that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And those troops that stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they stay under the banner of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Of course depends on the time-frame, but yes, through May they did. The time-frame of this resolution, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And post-May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: At some point in time, we were informed that in fact these troops had changed in effect the banner, as you called it, or the patch on their uniforms and in fact had redesignated themselves as the Army of Republika Srpska, and overnight or within a matter of minutes they had gone from being the Army of Yugoslavia, that is Serbian Montenegro, into the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was that information available to the Security Council or just to your government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That information was issued subsequently in a report to the Security Council which, to be very honest, at least caught me by surprise because we did not see a substantive withdrawal of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll come back to that issue in a moment, just for clarification, sir, but I want to look at one further part of this resolution, which is found at numbered paragraph 4 on the second page of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was suppose to happen to the weaponry the JNA had in Bosnia-Herzegovina according to this provision?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Well, this was a key point, and it was certainly consistent with the arms embargo resolution which is that the weapons that were part of the JNA, and remember the JNA was of course an army of all Yugoslavia including its former republics, that is Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the weapons in fact were either supposed to be left within the authority of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or to be placed under United Nations monitoring or actually control, I shouldn't even say the monitoring. It was supposed to be delivered to the international body.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Does the provisions actually indicate the weapons are to be left under the authority of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It says "... or subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or be disbanded and disarmed with their weapons placed under effective international monitoring." The point was that since we were the legal authority we, of course, had the right to those weapons if in fact the international did not take control of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I believe that document is already an exhibit in these proceedings, so if I could ask you to turn to the next document in your binder. Sorry, actually to tab 3 in your binder, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- which is 65 ter 9183. You should have a document before you that appears to have a date of 27 May, 1992, you described as a letter from the Charge d'affair of the permanent mission of the government of Yugoslavia. Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Who authored this -- first, do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The first page looks like it's signed by Dragomir Dzokic, and then there is an annex which is signed by Branko Kostic. Who is Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: As outlined in the document, he's vice-president at the time of the Serbian Montenegro, the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You said you recognised this document, where did you recognise it from, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I actually received -- excuse me, I'm rushing into your answers. I apologise to the interpreters. I recognise it as having in fact been relevant to the discussion as to whether or not the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, the JNA forces had withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of this document back in May 1992, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You are kindly requested to switch off your microphones while not using them, you are also kindly requested to pause between questions and answers. Interpreters are having a lot of background noise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, you can speak now.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, I actually -- I remember seeing it several days, well, a day or two after it was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, there's three aspects of this document I'd like to discuss with you. The first aspect you'll find at -- the first aspect you've already averted to, which is the issue of whether they were complying with Resolution 752. And if I could turn your attention to page 3, there is a paragraph and that -- sorry, is page 3 of the entire document, is page 2 of the annex. And there's a paragraph that starts with the word "thirdly"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. There is an indication here -- the text reads: "Thirdly, the Presidency of Yugoslavia decided on the day of the promulgation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is on 27th April, 1992, that it would reduce the Army of Yugoslavia to the territory and citizens of Yugoslavia. As a result, all of the citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who had been in the YPA, Yugoslav People's Army, troops, in that republic were withdrawn by 19th May, 1992, together with their share of equipment and armaments." I'm going to ask about that last phrase, "together with their share of equipment and armaments." Had there been any discussion at the Security Council surrounding Resolution 752 to suggest that the JNA was entitled to take with it a share of equipment and armaments?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all, there was no such discussion that in fact any of the military weapons would be left in the hands of those other than the legitimate government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As you can see from this paragraph, there is no reference to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They frequently just referred to that authority in Sarajevo as the Muslims. Second of all, you asked me if I had seen this letter before. I did not view it as being authoritative on the issue of whether or not the United Nations itself had in fact concluded that Resolution 752 had been complied with, and when I saw this letter, I did not believe that in fact that resolution had been complied with. And this particular paragraph it itself indicates that it had not been because it implies that in fact some of the weapons was not delivered either to international control, that is UN control, or to the control of the legitimate government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The second aspects of the letter I want to direct you to is the paragraph directly above the paragraph we've just been discussing, and that's the paragraph that starts with the word "secondly." The text reads: "Secondly" --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "... the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has demonstrated a maximum degree of tolerance with respect to the premature decisions on the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Could you tell me what we are talking about when we talk about a country being internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that we are asking the question in the same manner that we've asked it before which is factual and not legal in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Could you answer the question I posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. Any response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My friend was I thought asking for clarification that I was asking it as a factual question not as a legal question, I'm asking for his understanding of a term of art at the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith. I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I have an objection with regard to relevance of what his understanding of "a term of art at the UN" may be. It either has legal significance or it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject. This is the witness, Mr. Sacirbey, if I may interject, Your Honour, I can maybe help explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. You want to interject, Mr. Sacirbey, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I can help clarify the issue that seems to be coming back as to whether these are legal or factual issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you what do you want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course these issues have a legal context, but in fact I was dealing with them in the factual elements of the institutions within which I was working. Whether my legal interpretations were accurate or not, I don't believe is something that is particularly at issue here. It is in fact in how these matters were being handled in the context of my responsibilities as a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore that is what I am -- I believe I am addressing here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Would you like to perhaps find out how he handled it in his capacity as a representative of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain to me in terms of the job that you had to do as ambassador, was it significant to you whether or not Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised internationally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was very significant. First of all, every country that recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina then accredited it certain rights to Bosnia-Herzegovina, including treaty obligations, including various matters related to international relations, but most importantly, each country that recognizes Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time also recognizes its territorial integrity and sovereignty. From this then we could also develop our membership in international institution, including the United Nations. It would be very difficult for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be admitted to an international body like the United Nations unless there was either an existing recognition or an intent to recognise Bosnia within its existing borders, its territorial integrity. Also, Bosnia when it in fact applies for membership, commits itself to abide by the rules of that international institution and also to respect the territorial integrity and sovereignty of neighbouring states. In particular in this context we represented on numerous occasions that we would respect the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Serbian Montenegro; that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At any point during the conflict, so 1992 to 1995, did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia reciprocate and recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was it ever called upon to do so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: First of all by Bosnia-Herzegovina, and second of all by other international institutions or let's say member states.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: During the conflict, did you become aware at any point in time of the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but to be more accurate, we understood it as strategic objectives of Serbian Montenegro along with their allies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What do you recall as some of those objectives being?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not quite sure whether you are on the same page. Your question was about strategic objectives of Bosnian Serbs, the answer was: "We understood it as strategic objectives of Serbian Montenegro along with their allies in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, I will clarify, Your Honour. I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about the allies of Serbian Montenegro in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We refer today them frequently, to be again more accurate, I appreciate Your Honour's comment as well, as their agents. Sometimes we would refer to them as the Pale Serbs. Sometimes we would refer to them by the general designation of Serbian. We actually did not refer to them as representing all of the Bosnian Serbs and did not accredit them that view.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So when I speak about the Bosnian Serbs, would you equate that with the term Pale Serbs that you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. We did not wish to give this conflict the perspective of an ethnic or religious conflict which we believe the other side did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So going back then to what you understood were these joint objectives shared by - according to your understanding - both Serbian Montenegro and the forces in Pale, led by Pale, what do you recall about those objectives?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: To put it in very broad terms, and you will please ask me to specify it if anything more is needed, it is a Greater Serbia with contiguous, that is, continuous borders, that in fact there would not be an internationally recognised border between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbian Montenegro. We also recognised that the territorial ambitions were rather dynamic, to use that term. In fact, that the -- if in -- I understood that in fact if all of Bosnia was conquered that in fact it all would become part of some Republika Srpska and that in fact that would become all part of some Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have indicated that you believed there was commonality and objectives between the government and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the forces in Pale. My question is if the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that have had any impact on the ability to realise what you consider to be or what you believe to be the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That question is both speculative and vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, would you like to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The witness seems to have not had any difficulty in answering the question, Your Honour. And if the response he gives indicates that he did not -- that he thought the question was too vague, then we will ask follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I find -- I don't see the vagueness. Let the witness answer and we'll hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But -- a two-part objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are saying, Mr. Guy-Smith. You gave us one objection, now you're saying two-part objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I gave you two objections. I said it was speculative and it was vague. The question is -- is speculative and it is vague. Thus far, we've dealt with the issue of it being vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to say anything about speculation, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In my view it doesn't call on him to speculate. The question calls on him to give an answer, and if he can't give an answer that isn't based on speculation then he will so indicate, Your Honour, but he started to answer without any difficulty before my friend interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a classic issue, when somebody asks a question that has within it the word "if" it is by definition speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The basis for this question, as I understand it, is that the witness has testified that the strategic objective was that if the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina could be conquered, it would be made part of a Greater Serbia. Now, obviously if Bosnia-Herzegovina is recognised, I guess it's a question of logical deduction whether or not the strategic objective has been achieved or not. And whether the question is put or not, as I say, it's a very logical deduction and I don't think it's speculation. From that point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're dealing with the issue of the -- in -- and you see, the problem is that you're dealing with the issue of the impact. The question is the impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's fine. The impact on the strategic objective. The question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You may not have heard His Honour, Mr. Sacirbey, he indicated the question was allowed, so could you continue your answer unless you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We certainly felt that the issue had merit in blunting the objectives on any Greater Serbia, because the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by Serbian Montenegro, that is at that time the government in Belgrade, would have at least in the context of international legal terms prohibited any or all of Bosnia-Herzegovina being somehow in the future annexed into a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I just want you to skip ahead in time for a moment to the talks that preceded the Dayton Accord. Did you participate in those talks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, as foreign minister of Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at those peace talks around this issue of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. To be more precise on the point, the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in fact a critical point with the negotiations and it concluded with Serbian Montenegro recognising the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were, I must add, some efforts there to also though, at least on the part of Belgrade, which was presumably negotiating on behalf of the Pale Serbs, to bring about a referendum in the so-called Republika Srpska at that time that would allow for Republika Srpska to declare its decision to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina and presumably would be allowed to join at that time Belgrade, that is Serbian Montenegro. This point ultimately was not left in the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who on behalf of Belgrade at Dayton was advancing the position that there ought to be a possibility of a referendum on cessation in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, this point was addressed to us through many negotiations leading up to Dayton, but in particularly in Dayton it was the delegation of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could return to the text of the letter, the final aspect I want to discuss is the issue of paragraph -- page 4, the first paragraph. So if you would turn the page from the page that we've been dealing with. The very first --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The very first paragraph says: "The option of sanctions against Yugoslavia on the basis of unsubstantiated claims of aggression is deeply unfair and wrong. History knows of no case of a country threatening another without using the army. As of 19th May this year, not a single soldier who is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia remains in that republic, and the borders with Bosnia and Herzegovina have been closed for 30 days now for any crossings of armed individuals or groups who might try to make them." My question to you is this: The text suggests that the options of sanctions was being discussed against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the basis of claims of aggression. Does that fairly represent what was in fact happening in the discussions of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: We referenced both aggression as well as, of course, grey violations of an international humanitarian law, that is, acts against our citizens as I've referred to by the term ethnic purification or genocide. And I will also note that of course this paragraph does not in any way reference the delivery of military goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure your answer was responsive to my question, which was in the context of discussions surrounding Resolution 752 --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- does this text accurately summarise the reason why sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were being considered?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They were being considered for two reasons. One of them is aggression, that is interference into the affairs or more correctly violations of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of a neighbouring state, that is Serbian Montenegro violating the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and second, of course, was the implications that this had in terms of the population. Violations of international humanitarian law, i.e., genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the means by which the government of Serbian Montenegro was allegedly engaged in aggression and interfering with the affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The first would have been through its military forces, that is regular military forces. The second one would have been para-military forces that came from Serbian Montenegro, which I believe the Court is familiar with. And the third would have been, of course, actual raids across the border conducted by military forces including air power from one side of the border to the next. I guess the fourth we would say is the supply of goods to whatever we designate those forces within Bosnia to be to carry out this aggression and to carry out the attacks upon the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the letter that was sent that we've been discussing, were the sanctions in fact adopted against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could this document we've been discussing please be marked as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next -- one moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Yes, if you could turn to the next tab in your binder being tab 4, you should have in front of you a one-page document which is Exhibit P334 in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you just take a moment and look at that. It's -- if you could just read that to yourself for a moment, sir. Yes, you've read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were telling us earlier about your recollection of some strategic objectives you became aware of during the conflict. How does the text of this document compare to your recollection of what you became aware of during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It is very consistent in that it outlines what is called the strategic objectives for the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as you can see, there are many demarcation lines even left open including particularly what I note here as Point 6: Access to the sea for Republika Srpska, which means that this seem to be a rather open ended plan for the creation and expansion in effect of Republika Srpska with few limitations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you ever saw this text while this conflict was ongoing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing it at the time. Certainly I was aware of these provisions, but I do not recall seeing this text at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you indicate approximately what the time-period was when you first became aware of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was actually quite in the beginning of probably in the early summer, late spring of 1992. We certainly referenced these in the context of the Greater Serbia and we used that term quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn, sir, to a different exhibit. The tab 7 in your binder, which is Prosecution Exhibit 202 in these proceedings, Resolution 757 of the Security Council. Do you have that document before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We were talking a few minutes ago about the fact that notwithstanding the letter from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia some sanctions were imposed against the fellow Republic of Yugoslavia. My first question with respect to this document is were you present when it was debated and passed? When this resolution was debated and passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the date this was passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to the third page of this resolution where there are again numbered paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm looking at numbered paragraph 1. There is a condemnation of a failure of the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to take effective measures to fulfill the requirements of Resolution 752. What requirements of Resolution 752 did the Security Council determine had not been complied with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Well, as you have, I believe, indicated, despite the previous letter from the authorities, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in fact there had been failure to withdraw the Yugoslav People's Army from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at beginning at paragraph 4 there is a text which starts with the words "decides that all states shall prevent" then there's a series of subparagraphs and other paragraphs that follows. What was the effect of this resolution? What was were the -- sorry, what was -- what did the UN Security Council resolve to do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: One of them was to obviously provide sanctions, but as importantly, or more importantly, it was particularly to focus on military goods that could be used to contribute to the war effort led against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was the -- when you talk about sanctions, who was being sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: In this case it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbian Montenegro, if you would, the government in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the sanctions that the Security Council imposed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They had clearly political economic implications. Political in the sense that a country should never want to be sanctioned, especially under Chapter 7. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I think -- I'm interrupting because I think you've misunderstood my question. What kinds of sanctions --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What kinds of sanctions was the Security Council imposing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: They were imposing mandatory sanctions under Chapter 7, number one, so these were not voluntary to member states, they were mandatory, which means that each member state had to comply with the provision as it relates to their dealing with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Number 2, they in fact prevented certain goods, transshipments, dealings with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, some in a more general economic nature, some very specific to products, if you would, goods that could be used, particularly in a military capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of the economic sanctions, what was -- what were the most important elements of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Particularly trade, and transshipment of goods and of course even financial implications for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the context of the discussions that have resulted in passing of this resolution, was there any discussion of how imposing economic and other sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was going to improve matters in the region?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: By looking it at the resolution itself, it outlined - particularly the previous paragraphs - it outlined why in fact the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was being sanctioned, i.e., that it had not met its obligations under the previous resolution mentioned. And as a consequence, the desired objective was to compel the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to comply with that resolution, particularly as it relates to its -- the presence of its forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the actions of those forces both on the issue of aggression, but also the issue of engaging in acts that violated the rights, that is, violated and endangered of course and in many cases inflicted harm upon the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was this the only resolution imposing sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was passed by the Security Council during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: No, there were actually several more, quite a few more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there discussion in the context of those additional sanctions, which I promise we will discuss in a little more detail later, was there discussion of what the UN Security Council hoped to achieve by sanctioning the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Both in the context of the resolution, but also in the context of the statements made by member states of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So what was the end goal of imposing sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: To cease their direct and indirect actions as they in fact continued to fuel not only the conflict, but also, if you would the aggression, but also to in fact cease those actions that caused such harm to the population, as we have come to call them ethnic cleansing. And also to bring about a normalization of the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbian Montenegro. This is, of course, a reference to the issue of mutual recognition, and the respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty and the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You talk about compelling the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to cease their indirect actions. What are you talking about? What was being alleged?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Certainly we always knew that there were troops being sent into Bosnia and coming out. We also know that there were in fact various goods of military value being sent into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also so-called para-military forces were given largely free rein to go in and conduct ethnic cleansing and brutal campaigns, and in fact there may have been even what one could consider political actions by were contrary to the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina including, of course, the failure to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was the thinking at the UN Security Council in terms of what would happen if you could successfully eliminate the contributions that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was alleged to be making to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if that's covered by a resolution, that's one matter. But now we are dealing with the entire thinking of the UN Security Council. The question as is presently posed is vague and I think is outside the ken of this particular witness's ability to answer what the thinking was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there discussion in the context of the UN Security Council as to what was hoped to be achieved by eliminating the contributions that were allegedly being made by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It was the thinking of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and reflected by many of the member states of the UN Security Council and other independent observers that without the support, direct and indirect support of Belgrade, there in fact were no viable Pale Serb forces. That is, the war would in fact be extinguished.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that was the thinking of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you share that strategy or thinking with any members of the UN Security Council or the council as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And vice-versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did any of that -- did any of that thinking occur in the context of discussions of proposed -- or any of that discussion occur in the context of proposed resolutions sanctioning the Federal Government of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct. Since the objective was to end the war, to end the ethnic cleansing, obviously the resolutions were designed to stop, to impede Belgrade's continued direct and indirect support.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics a little, sir, and discuss Sarajevo which we've only touched on very briefly. Could you tell me what the situation in Sarajevo was in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: It dramatically changed from, let's say, mid-spring, that is April, particularly after sniper attacks upon a peaceful March of individuals calling for no war in Bosnia. Several people were killed at that point in time, and very quickly Sarajevo came under siege. By late that spring, it was very difficult, if not impossible, to come or leave Sarajevo for normal citizens. And by the end of that period, which you're referring to, Sarajevo was in a very troubled humanitarian situation. Very limited, if any, access, not only to food and medicines, but even to water.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Under which forces were laying siege to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The Serbian forces. And these forces particularly at that time not only had encircled the city, but in fact were very frequently involved in military actions from not only sniper fire, but obviously bombardment. And it was, from what I can tell, it was rather indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was the topic of the bombardment of Sarajevo and sniper fire, sniper attacks in Sarajevo, were those topics discussed at all in the UN Security Council in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, starting in the spring of 1992, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just focusing on the spring and the summer of 1992, how frequently were those topics being discussed at either the UN Security Council or the General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I would say almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the Security Council pass any resolutions dealing with Sarajevo in that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I think it's safe enough to say that the resolutions we have discussed already in fact did incorporate Sarajevo, because in part the demand to withdraw the JNA troops was related to lifting the siege of Sarajevo, and then of course it continued on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Other than the resolutions we've already discussed, were there any other resolutions passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but I'll need to refresh my memory as to the exact time-frame that you want me to address here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to identify some documents, sir. You should still be in tab 7, and if you turn the page to the end of the document we've just been discussing we should have --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- document 65 ter 2075.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And those are titled Security Council Resolutions 758, 760, and 761.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just refresh your memory, sir, as to whether these resolutions all or any individual ones dealt with the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. At this point in time the issue of actually delivering humanitarian assistance, and even the ability of the international community to have access to Sarajevo and monitor the situation had come into play. These resolutions dealt with that. So we are going from resolutions that dealt with the effect of siege of Sarajevo by the JNA forces to the humanitarian situation, and even to the point where the international can in fact observe and act in its ability or its mandate to improve that humanitarian situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just ask that this -- these three resolutions be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will become Exhibit P2434, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 8, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You see Resolution 764, which is 65 ter 2069. Do you have that document, sir?
