utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at the text of this document, two parts I want to refer you to, sir. The first is the second column on the first page. There's a paragraph that starts with the words "deeply disturbed."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Deeply disturbed by the situation which now prevails in Sarajevo and by many reports and indications of deteriorating conditions throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then if you would turn the page there is paragraph -- numbered paragraphs and numbered paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Numbered paragraph 10 indicates: "Reaffirms that all parties are bound to comply with the obligations under international and humanitarian law and in particular the Geneva Conventions of 12th August 1949, and that persons who commit to order the commission of grave breaches of the Conventions are individually responsible in respect of such breaches." Was this resolution passed or triggered by any particular event or events?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think to tie into your questions now overall, around this same period of time we had what's referred to generally as the bread-line massacre, which was widely seen in the media where dozens of people had been murdered by the indiscriminate shelling of civilians lined up to receive bread within the town of Sarajevo. During this period of time, the humanitarian conditions had really come to deteriorate in terms to access to food, medicine, water. There were lots of reports not only of sniping, but shelling. And in particular, there were reports -- I shouldn't say reports, that confirmed of course information, of individuals from certain parts of Sarajevo, and Sarajevo's made up into a municipal unit, certain parts of that municipal unit in fact had been ethnically cleansed, and most of that population had been forced out of their homes. Many actually, at least for some time detained, put into various camps, some deported outside the country, others managed to come into the territory at that time held by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time we were also obviously demanding greater action from the international community, to undertake political and/or military action to lift the siege of Sarajevo, and the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was also the time the French President Mitterrand had flown into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Just dealing with the text where there is discussion or reminding that the parties are bound to comply with international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions, was there discussion of whether any of the events that you have articulated were being reported, for example, shelling of people standing in a bread line, sniper attacks, was there a discussion of whether those incidents would constitute breaches of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was, as you said, shelling, sniping. There was attacks upon neighbourhood, that is where people were actually then expelled from their home, and of course, there was a denial of those necessities of life, whether it was foods, medicines, or water. And in fact, there was a denial of movement within the city because the city was surrounded and besieged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of the involvement of the FRY delegation and the meeting that resulted in Resolution 764, was the FRY delegation represented to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you raise the issue of either the bread-line massacre or the siege generally with the delegation, the mission, FRY mission in New York?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I did and my staff. Just to add to your point before, by then in fact our staff had expanded to several individuals although we were still working out of my private business office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You mentioned that the bread-line massacre was widely reported in the media. How much media attention did events in Sarajevo attract generally between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Tremendous amount. I don't think I was necessarily biased in that perspective. It was rather impossible to ignore, almost in any news report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how much communication did you have, if any, as the Bosnian ambassador with the press?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Extensive at that time. I probably was giving several interviews a day, maybe four, five, six on the average.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there any accredited journalists at the United Nations from within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I seem to recall at least two most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would you by chance remember anyone's name or what agency they worked for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: I don't remember names to be very honest with you, but I do remember that they worked for -- sometimes they were pool reporters and sometimes they were specifically associated with some of the largest media, that is publications in Belgrade. I also, by the way, spoke directly sometimes to Belgrade itself, to the media there that called me, including B92, the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of your communications with the media, you've indicated you gave interviews. Did you ever give press conferences or hold press conferences?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Generally, those conferences were scheduled in what is known as the United Nations press room. Again, right there in UN headquarters, very close to the Security Council Chamber. Those were formal press conferences, and there usually would actually be sent a schedule indicating that a conference would be held, and we usually tried to alert the media at least several hours -- more likely a day or two in advance, but at least several hours. Other times in front of the United Nations Security Council, as is the practice today, there would be in fact impromptu press conferences with most of the UN media core present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could try to keep your answers short, we have a lot of territory to cover. With respect to the press conferences, could you tell us if they were attended by the media representatives you told us were accredited at the UN from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Both the formal and informal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you or any of your staff make any effort during the conflict to monitor what was being reported in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Particularly one of my deputies, Ivan Misic, was a former reporter, so he paid special attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were allegations of shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo reported in the media in Belgrade or elsewhere in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Certainly sometimes, and certainly even in the direct reports that I gave to, let's say, a station like B92, I'm very well aware that they were reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about other allegations of ethnic cleansing by the Serbian forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: That is correct, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to tab 9, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that last document should be tendered as an exhibit if it hasn't already been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has not yet. It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should see before in tab 9 three documents, the first of which is 65 ter 3763.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a document titled "A Note by the President of the Security Council." What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Sometimes the president of the Security Council would make a statement on behalf of the entire membership of the UN Security Council, that was in lieu of a resolution or more accurately reflected a consensus of the Security Council members. It did not have the weight of a resolution, but in fact, it did have an indication of the thinking of the Security Council as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. This text that this document refers at paragraph 3 to continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law, and in particular reports of the imprisonment and abuse of civilians in camps. What was -- what is this resolution or sorry, this statement referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: This is the time when we started to receive very clear evidence, pictures, not just newspaper accounts, but even pictures and TV footage of Bosnia-Herzegovinian citizens being held in detention in what I think one can label as concentration camps or detention camps. And there were, of course, other reports of continued ethnic cleansing, removal of people from their homes, and of course reports of individuals or actually groups being murdered. I say groups, because many of the reports that we received were large scale and systemic killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina citizen, who was reportedly detained in these camps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: The non-Serb population, Bosniaks, that is Bosnian Muslim and Croats, but there were also sometimes Serbs who opposed the regime or opposed the efforts of division of Belgrade who were also in fact made to suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you talked about there being pictures and TV footage, how widely publicised were the images of the camps at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: At this point in time, this dominated the news, the global news.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that document be marked as an exhibits please, and could you turn to the next document in that tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The next document, and there's two more documents in this tab. One is 65 ter 2192, which is Resolution 770.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to that resolution, I don't want to discuss it in any detail, I'd just like you to take a look at the text and confirm for me whether this appears to be a true copy of the actual resolution that was passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think that would - actually, I see the time, Your Honour - be a convenient time to break and we'll deal with the other resolution tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. Just before we break, Mr. Sacirbey, while you are in the witness-stand, just to remind you, you may not discuss the case with anybody, not even with your counsel there in the US, until you are excused from testifying. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is recognised, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Chamber stands adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. That's Netherlands time. In the same courtroom, I guess you will be in the same venue. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of June, 2009, at 2.00 p.m. 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
